title: Tardigrades: Nature's Cuddly, Indestructible Microanimal
summary: Josh and Chuck explain tardigrades (water bears), tiny multicellular micro-animals roughly half a millimeter to a millimeter long, with a phylum of their own, found in moss, lichen and water across the planet. They cover their eight stubby legs, open circulatory system, and their three states (active, cryptobiosis/tun state, anoxybiosis). The hosts describe their extreme tolerance of freezing near absolute zero, boiling heat, high pressure, radiation, vacuum and space exposure, plus how they protect DNA (Dsup protein) and repair it. They discuss the debunked 2014-era claim of widespread foreign gene transfer from a contaminated sample, the Japanese revival of moss-dwelling tardigrades stored for decades, and the question of why these traits evolved. The episode ends with a listener mail about Aaron Sorkin's dialogue style and a sign-off.

segments.title: Introduction to tardigrades
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce tardigrades as tiny, cute, ancient micro-animals that have gained internet popularity, and mention names like water bear and moss piglet.

segments.title: Discovery, naming and anatomy
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Latin name meaning slow walker, given by Lazzaro Spallanzani after earlier discovery by Johann Goeze, the history of microscope observation, their eight stubby legs with claws, and their open circulatory system and simple organs. They note the range of habitats in moss, lichen and water and their phylum status.

segments.title: Species diversity and reproduction
segments.summary: They note around a thousand species, mostly land, marine and freshwater, with varied reproduction including egg-laying, sexual and self-fertilizing species, and diets of plant or animal fluids, including cannibalism.

segments.title: Extreme temperature, pressure and radiation tolerance
segments.summary: The hosts cover tardigrades surviving near absolute zero, being boiled at about 150 C, enduring pressures six times greater than Earth's deepest, gamma and X-ray radiation (a French study on lethal doses), and space exposure, with scientists unsure how their cells avoid freezing damage.

segments.title: Anhydrobiosis, cryptobiosis and dormant states
segments.summary: The hosts describe anoxybiosis from oxygen starvation and cryptobiosis (the tun state) when dried, with metabolism falling to a small fraction, and revival of moss samples after decades including a claimed 120-year-old sample and 32-year survival.

segments.title: Thomas Boothby, gene transfer controversy and Ramazzottius research
segments.summary: Thomas Boothby's team reported many foreign genes, which turned out to be contamination; the hosts discuss the follow-up study of Ramazzottius varieornatus showing about one percent foreign genes, and anti-freeze proteins not being produced.

segments.title: Evolution question and closing tangents
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether tardigrades are aliens or came from asteroids, noting they would burn up on re-entry, and conclude their survival traits are likely from DNA repair ability rather than a purpose. A tangent about cold butter and Nerf guns follows.

segments.title: Listener mail: Aaron Sorkin
segments.summary: A listener named Mark Frost defends Aaron Sorkin's stylized dialogue, comparing it to musicals and Shakespeare, and discusses the Steve Jobs film; the hosts recommend The Night Manager.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and point to social media and the website for more.
